entities.name: Edinburgh Festival Theatre
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Edinburgh Festival Theatre, reopened in 1994 after restoration of a 1928 cinema in the Scottish capital, is the largest theater in Scotland (1,915 seats) and anchor venue for Edinburgh's extraordinary festival culture — a city whose annual August festivals (International, Fringe, Book, Art) constitute the world's largest arts festival, attracting 4+ million visitors and presenting 50,000+ performances across 300+ venues in one month. Edinburgh's festival ecosystem has made it the second-largest arts economy in the UK after London.

The building's history reflects Scottish cultural history: opened as the Empire Palace (1892), converted to the Empire Cinema (1928), then restored as the Edinburgh Festival Theatre (1994) with a distinctive glass-and-steel facade inserted into the Victorian auditorium. The Edinburgh International Festival (founded 1947 by Rudolf Bing, Bruno Walter, and others as postwar cultural healing) was almost immediately accompanied by the unofficial Fringe (1947) when theater companies arrived uninvited — establishing the pattern of official and unofficial parallel festivals.

The Edinburgh Fringe (since 1947) has grown to the world's largest arts festival: in 2019, 3,841 shows in 323 venues across 25 days, with 3 million ticket purchases. The Fringe launch-pad effect — where successful productions transfer to London, Broadway, and international tours — has made Edinburgh the most important talent development venue in the English-speaking world. Richard Bean, James Graham, and countless stand-up comedians were discovered or advanced through Edinburgh. The Festival Theatre itself presents opera, dance, ballet, and major productions from international companies.
